in_context.text: Paul is listing the qualities a church overseer ("bishop") must have. Verse 4 says he must rule his own house well, with his children in order. Verse 5 is a short aside in parentheses giving the reason: a man who cannot manage his own home is not ready to care for God's church.

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote it in Paul's name, while others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul had left to lead the church at Ephesus.

affected.text: Men who desire the office of overseer, and the church they would care for. Deacons are held to a similar standard about their homes in verse 12.

what.text: The verse is a reasoned question, not a new rule. It argues from the smaller to the larger: a man's home life shows whether he can lead and care for the church.

events.text: The text does not tie this instruction to a specific event. It is part of Paul's guidance for setting up leaders in the Ephesian church.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's first and second Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110.

where.text: The letter was sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia. Where Paul wrote from is not stated, though it may have been Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul wants Timothy to choose leaders of proven character. Managing a household well is evidence that a man can be trusted with the church.

big_picture.text: Paul calls the church "the house of God" in verse 15, so the home and the church are compared directly. A man who leads his own house well is fit to help care for God's house.

for_readers.text: Character shown at home matters for leading the church. 1 Samuel gives a warning: God judged a house "because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not."

christians_differ.text: Traditions differ on what the "bishop" (overseer) office is. Some see it as a distinct, higher office over several churches. Others treat it as the same role as elder or pastor, noting that in Acts 20:28 Paul calls the Ephesian elders "overseers." Readers also differ on whether this verse requires a leader to be married with children, or simply requires that any household he has be well managed.

why_it_matters.text: The word means to stand before or preside over. It describes leading from the front, the same word used of church leaders elsewhere (Romans 12:8; 1 Timothy 5:17).
Paul shifts from "rule" to "take care of" when he speaks of the church. This verb is used elsewhere in the New Testament only in Luke 10:34-35.
The word means a house or household. Paul uses the same idea for the church as "the house of God" in verse 15, which is what makes the comparison work.
The word means an assembly or congregation. Here it is the gathered people of God, not a building.

takeaway.text: Leading God's people is like leading a family, only larger. Paul asks how a man who cannot rule his own house could take care of the church of God.
